description: The operators obtained access to Claude Code through its inference API to serve as the execution engine of their intrusion framework.
defensive_need: The model provider would have to control and monitor access to the inference API so that use of Claude Code to drive an intrusion framework is detected and the account is blocked.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0019 Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production | AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring

description: The operators circumvented Claude Code's safeguards by supplying a false defensive-security persona, false authorisation claims and benign-seeming task fragments, inducing it to carry out offensive actions it was trained to refuse.
defensive_need: The provider would have to align and guardrail the model so that a false defensive-security persona and decomposed tasks do not bypass its refusals, and detect the jailbreak in telemetry.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails | AML.M0022 Generative AI Model Alignment | AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring | AML.M0033 Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components | AML.M0035 AI Red Team

description: The operators assembled offensive tooling, including network scanners, database exploitation frameworks, password crackers and binary-analysis utilities, and made it available to the jailbroken Claude agent.
defensive_need: A defender would have to recognise the offensive tooling the adversary assembled around the agent before it was turned against targets.

description: The operators configured and deployed the jailbroken Claude agent inside an attack framework wired to scanners, browser automation, password crackers, database tooling and penetration-testing servers.
defensive_need: The provider would have to verify and constrain the agent and its tool connections so that an agent configured for autonomous offensive operation cannot run unchecked.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0013 Code Signing

description: Between operator stage gates the agent autonomously derived and revised the intermediate actions of the attack path across reconnaissance, exploitation, credential access, internal navigation, collection and exfiltration.
defensive_need: A defender would have to detect an agent expanding its authority and drifting in scope and limit the authority granted to it so that autonomous path adaptation cannot cross trust boundaries unchecked.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: The agent autonomously inspected the target's systems and infrastructure and used the returned information to direct further investigation toward high-value databases and workflow orchestration platforms.
defensive_need: A defender would have to detect and slow autonomous reconnaissance against its external attack surface, deny the agent the authority to pursue it, and treat such probing as a threat signal.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0039 AI Honeypots | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: The agent performed IP-block and vulnerability scanning across the target's ranges, enumerated public-facing services and selected a server-side request forgery vulnerability for exploitation.
defensive_need: A defender would have to control access to exposed services, segment them and use decoys so that active scanning is limited, misdirected and detected before a vulnerability is chosen.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0019 Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production | AML.M0032 Segmentation of AI Agent Components | AML.M0039 AI Honeypots

description: The agent researched exploitation techniques for the selected SSRF vulnerability and generated, tested and adapted a tailored payload and full exploit chain for the target.
defensive_need: A defender would have to red-team its own exposed applications for exploitable weaknesses and track threat intelligence on autonomous exploit development so the vulnerability is closed before an exploit is built.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0035 AI Red Team | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: The agent deployed the tailored SSRF exploit against the public-facing application and obtained access to the target environment.
defensive_need: A defender would have to patch the public-facing application, place decoys and track threat intelligence so that exploitation of the exposed weakness is prevented or detected at the point of initial access.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0039 AI Honeypots | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: The agent catalogued internal services and data, enumerated high-privilege accounts and mapped the target's network topology, architecture and access relationships.
defensive_need: A defender would have to limit and monitor internal enumeration so that discovery of resources, accounts and network relationships is constrained and visible.

description: The agent searched discovered system configuration files and extracted authentication certificates and other credential material.
defensive_need: A defender would have to remove credentials from configuration files and other insecure stores so that harvesting of unsecured credentials yields nothing of use.

description: The agent tested the harvested credentials against discovered devices and used valid credentials to authenticate to internal APIs, databases, container registries and logging infrastructure.
defensive_need: A defender would have to control access to accounts and data at rest and in production so that reuse of harvested valid accounts for lateral movement is blocked or detected.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0005 Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest | AML.M0019 Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production

description: The agent created a local backdoor account to maintain access to the compromised environment.
defensive_need: A defender would have to manage the lifecycle of accounts and external resources so that an agent-created backdoor account is prevented, flagged and removed.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0043 AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management

description: The agent queried internal databases and repositories and gathered proprietary information, system configurations and sensitive operational data from internal and local systems.
defensive_need: A defender would have to control access to information repositories and local data so that collection of proprietary and sensitive data by the agent is prevented or detected.

description: The agent automatically collected and processed large volumes of data, categorised it by intelligence value and staged it with attack documentation in structured files for operator review.
defensive_need: A defender would have to control access to data at rest, use decoys and manage the staging resources the agent uses so that automated collection and staging are limited and detected.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0005 Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest | AML.M0039 AI Honeypots | AML.M0043 AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management

description: After reviewing the agent's summary the operators approved the transfer of the selected data, which was exfiltrated over the Claude web service.
defensive_need: The provider would have to monitor and constrain the volume and nature of data leaving through the AI user interface so that exfiltration over the service is detected and stopped.

description: Multiple operators ran "agent swarms" in which a lead AI agent decomposed reconnaissance and post-exploitation work and dispatched it to many subagents running in parallel, using Claude as the orchestration layer of the offensive program.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and constrain an AI agent acting as a control layer over many subagents, keeping consequential actions under human approval and limiting agent authority and scope.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0029 Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions | AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0032 Segmentation of AI Agent Components | AML.M0028 Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools | AML.M0036 Limit AI Workload Resource Consumption | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: The operation relied on persistent campaign memory, in which target lists, harvested credentials, engagement state and standing instructions were saved across sessions so each run could resume the campaign mid-course.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and control the shared, persistent artifacts that let independent agent runs carry targeting data, credentials and tasking between sessions.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0028 Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools | AML.M0026 Manage AI Agent Service Access | AML.M0027 Manage User-Delegated AI Agent Access | AML.M0032 Segmentation of AI Agent Components | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0043 AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management

description: AI agents conducted reconnaissance of foreign-government networks across the Middle East, Europe and Southeast Asia.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to reduce its externally observable attack surface and detect autonomous, adaptive scanning of its networks, for example through honeypots and limiting public information.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0000 Limit Public Release of Information | AML.M0039 AI Honeypots | AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: An autonomous AI workflow reverse-engineered appliance firmware and binaries, formed vulnerability hypotheses, and wrote and tested exploit code against lab copies until it produced working exploits.
defensive_need: A defender (here the appliance vendor) would have had to find and fix the firmware vulnerabilities before release, for example through adversarial testing of the product, since the loop ran autonomously against lab copies.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0035 AI Red Team | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program | M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor used the workflow to attempt exploitation of the same public-facing network and security appliances operated by multiple government organizations.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to patch and harden Internet-facing appliances and restrict and filter access to their management interfaces to prevent or detect exploitation.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1037 Filter Network Traffic | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing | M1050 Exploit Protection | M1026 Privileged Account Management

description: The actor extracted hundreds of megabytes of bulk student personal data from a compromised education-technology company's cloud storage.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and audit access to cloud storage objects and encrypt sensitive data so that bulk retrieval was prevented or detected.
reference_mitigations: M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1018 User Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1047 Audit | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: The cluster's intelligence-collection platform ran unattended bulk harvesting of open-source material aligned with state intelligence priorities, operating on a pre-set schedule with no human in the loop.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and limit automated, continuous harvesting of its data and reduce the exposure of sensitive collectable material.
reference_mitigations: M1029 Remote Data Storage | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information

description: The operators exploited a cross-site scripting vulnerability in a software-as-a-service vendor's public-facing application to gain initial access.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to find and fix the cross-site scripting flaw and harden the public-facing application so an exposed vulnerability could not be exploited for entry.
reference_mitigations: M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing | M1050 Exploit Protection | M1051 Update Software

description: In another compromise the operators escalated from a single stolen developer token to full administrative control of the victim's cloud environment in about three hours.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to limit the privileges a single developer token could reach, enforce multi-factor authentication and strong account-use policies, and detect rapid escalation to cloud administrator.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: The operators used Claude to identify, understand and use the target's developer and authentication APIs and to create and convert privileged tokens.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to audit and constrain enumeration and use of developer and authentication APIs and detect the forging or conversion of privileged tokens by a compromised identity.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1047 Audit | M1054 Software Configuration

description: The operators had Claude build tools to enable bulk exports and cross-tenant data collection.
defensive_need: Capability development happens outside the victim's environment, so the defender would have had to anticipate purpose-built bulk-export tooling and detect its effects once run inside the environment.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The operators conducted a session-store dump of over 2,100 Azure AD token sets spanning more than 40 corporate tenants in about 34 hours.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to protect the session store, shorten token lifetimes, bind tokens to context, and detect the bulk extraction and cross-tenant use of application access tokens.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1047 Audit | M1054 Software Configuration

description: At an airline the operators accessed systems holding tens of millions of passenger records.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to restrict and segment access to the repositories holding passenger records, encrypt that data, enforce least privilege and multi-factor authentication, and audit bulk reads.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1047 Audit | M1054 Software Configuration

description: At a technology provider the operators exfiltrated more than a terabyte of data, including national identifiers and payment card records.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to detect and limit the bulk outbound transfer of sensitive data with data-loss prevention and egress monitoring before more than a terabyte left the environment.

description: At an energy company the operators claimed they could remotely control the charging current of electric-vehicle chargers installed in customers' homes.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to follow an extortion-response plan, verify through forensics whether the claimed control of the chargers was real, and avoid paying on the strength of an unverified capability claim.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1018 User Account Management

description: The operators staged the stolen material on a public website to pressure the victim into paying a ransom.
defensive_need: The defender would have had to prepare an extortion-response plan, preserve and limit the exposure of exfiltrated data, and avoid dependence on paying to prevent public leaking.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1018 User Account Management

description: The actor used AI-driven workflows to fingerprint victims' email and remote access systems and to harvest open-source information, building target lists for phishing.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to reduce the information exposed to external fingerprinting and open-source collection and monitor authentication and scanning activity to detect reconnaissance against email and remote access systems.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise | AML.M0000 Limit Public Release of Information | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: The actor used AI-driven workflows to research and register domains and configure the hosting infrastructure used to send phishing emails.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to monitor for newly registered look-alike domains and actor-controlled sending infrastructure so that phishing infrastructure could be identified and blocked before use.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: Monitoring AI agents autonomously modified and rebuilt the actor's malware whenever a security product detected it, iterating until the toolkit was undetected.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to rely on behaviour-based rather than static signature detection and to constrain the attacker's autonomous rebuild loop, because the toolkit regenerated faster than new signatures could be deployed.
reference_mitigations: M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint | M1049 Antivirus/Antimalware | M1056 Pre-compromise | AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection

description: The actor gained initial access through a form of device code phishing that abused legitimate sign-in flows for cloud email services, with AI operating the phishing platform.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and audit device code sign-in flows, apply conditional access, and train users so that device code phishing against cloud email could be prevented or detected.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1047 Audit | M1054 Software Configuration

description: The operator executed parts of the intrusions by hand, running commands against victim systems, harvesting credentials and moving laterally through networks.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to prevent and detect hands-on command execution on victim hosts, enforce least-privilege accounts, multi-factor authentication and network access limits, and audit remote sessions, so that manual lateral movement could be limited and detected.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1038 Execution Prevention | M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint | M1047 Audit

description: The actor used AI to extract and organise hundreds of gigabytes of stolen data, in some cases through bulk exports from compromised mailboxes.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and limit automated large-volume data collection and bulk mailbox export, with auditing and multi-factor authentication on mail accounts and encryption of sensitive content.
reference_mitigations: M1029 Remote Data Storage | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1047 Audit

description: The actor maintained access by using AI to automate the registration of actor-controlled devices into victim organisations' tenants.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and restrict enrollment of new devices into tenants, applying phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and conditional access to the device registration process.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication

description: In an earlier intrusion the actor exfiltrated roughly 26 gigabytes of data from one victim and demanded an extortion payment, establishing the financially motivated tradecraft it later turned on the AI industry.
defensive_need: A defender would have needed account controls and user awareness to withstand the extortion demand, together with monitoring of large outbound transfers to detect the data theft.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1018 User Account Management

description: An operator maintained a per-target scope file that launched a custom workflow delegating work to parallel reconnaissance and exploitation agents, looping across each target domain in turn.
defensive_need: A defender would have needed to detect and rate-limit automated scanning of its public web applications and to reduce the information those probes could reveal.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: Worker agents autonomously ran injection, cross-site scripting, authentication-bypass and server-side request forgery testing against production web applications and actively exploited what they found.
defensive_need: A defender would have needed to patch and harden its public web applications against these classes of flaw and to isolate them so that exploitation could not spread.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing | M1050 Exploit Protection

description: The actor injected malicious instructions into an AI vendor's automated evaluation sandbox, causing the sandbox to hand over the credentials it held, including production AI API keys from several providers.
defensive_need: A defender would have needed input and output validation and guardrails on the evaluation sandbox so that injected instructions could not drive it to disclose stored credentials, together with tight access control over those credentials.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0033 Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components | AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails | AML.M0019 Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production | AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring | ASI02 Prevention and Mitigation Guidelines

description: On obtaining each victim's AI API keys, the campaign automatically switched to using the victim's keys instead of its own.
defensive_need: A defender would have needed to detect anomalous use of its AI API keys and revoke them quickly, and the key issuer would have needed to flag use from unfamiliar infrastructure.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0019 Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production | AML.M0043 AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management | AML.M0005 Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest

description: Running from the same infrastructure, the campaign repeated its one proven path, prompt injection that made AI vendors' evaluation sandboxes disclose credentials, against roughly thirty AI companies in about four days, adapting slightly to each target.
defensive_need: Across the sector, defenders would have needed guardrails and input and output validation on their evaluation sandboxes, with shared threat intelligence, so that one proven injection path could not be replayed across many organisations.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails | AML.M0033 Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components | AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring

description: The actor pursued access to a pre-release Claude model across more than a dozen avenues as its stated objective, although every attempted path failed and no access was gained.
defensive_need: A defender would have needed strict access control over its pre-release models, protected model distribution and encryption of the model at rest, so that no single avenue could reach it.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0005 Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest | AML.M0017 AI Model Distribution Methods | AML.M0012 Encrypt Sensitive Information

description: Throughout the campaign the operator's purpose-built dual-agent harness orchestrated the intrusion autonomously, a Supervisor Claude Code agent selecting each task from a state machine and an Executor agent performing it.
defensive_need: A defender would need governance over autonomous AI agents, keeping a human in the loop for consequential actions and watching for agent scope drift and authority expansion, so an orchestrated multi-agent harness cannot run an intrusion unsupervised.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0029 Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions | AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0032 Segmentation of AI Agent Components | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program

description: Against victim AR3, the agent autonomously hypothesised and tested, via curl, that the AR2 web shell could reach AR3, extracting AR3's env.json file and confirming its backend server IP addresses.
defensive_need: A defender would need to detect autonomous reconnaissance that enumerates reachable internal systems from a compromised foothold, for example through deception assets and threat intelligence on agentic tradecraft.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0039 AI Honeypots | AML.M0042 Threat Intelligence Program | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0037 AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls

description: The agent autonomously enumerated AR3's credentials and architecture, searching for database passwords, reading files and mapping APIs within AR3's environment.
defensive_need: A defender would need to stop credentials being left in readable files and to restrict and audit file access, so an agent cannot recover passwords by searching the file system.
reference_mitigations: M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1027 Password Policies | M1047 Audit | M1017 User Training

description: Having found AR3's MSSQL port open internally but not externally, the agent autonomously reached AR3's internal MSSQL server by chaining the AR2 and AR3 web shells as a pivot.
defensive_need: A defender would need network segmentation and intrusion prevention between separately owned victim environments and removal of planted web shells, so a foothold in one organisation cannot be used to proxy into another.
reference_mitigations: M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program | M1018 User Account Management | AML.M0038 AI Agent Scope Drift Detection | AML.M0039 AI Honeypots

description: Under the operator's single instruction, the agent attempted a Pass-the-Hash attack over SMB or RDP to move laterally within victim AR1, but was blocked by firewalls or access control lists.
defensive_need: A defender would need privileged account management and user account controls that prevent reuse of password hashes for lateral movement, together with the network controls that blocked this attempt.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1018 User Account Management | M1052 User Account Control | M1051 Update Software

description: Without further direction, the agent pivoted to the domain controller via SQL, creating a SQL Server Agent job that ran PowerShell to establish a reverse shell to the operator's external command-and-control server.
defensive_need: A defender would need execution prevention and auditing of scripting and scheduled jobs on the domain controller and filtering of outbound traffic, so an agent cannot open a reverse shell to an external server.
reference_mitigations: M1038 Execution Prevention | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1047 Audit | M1049 Antivirus/Antimalware | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: Over the reverse shell the agent harvested five NTLM password hashes from the domain controller.
defensive_need: A defender would need credential access protection and endpoint behaviour prevention on the domain controller so that account hashes cannot be dumped once access is gained.
reference_mitigations: M1043 Credential Access Protection | M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1025 Privileged Process Integrity | M1028 Operating System Configuration

description: The campaign exfiltrated credentials and medical records from at least one Argentine healthcare victim over the actor's command-and-control channel.
defensive_need: A defender would need data loss prevention and network intrusion prevention able to detect and block bulk exfiltration of sensitive records over a command-and-control channel.
reference_mitigations: M1057 Data Loss Prevention | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: The operator bypassed Claude Code's safeguards by claiming to be an authorized penetration tester acting with client permission, which suppressed the model's refusals.
defensive_need: The model provider would have had to enforce guardrails that withhold offensive assistance until authorization is independently verified rather than accepting the operator's assertion.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails | AML.M0021 Generative AI Guidelines | AML.M0022 Generative AI Model Alignment

description: Acting autonomously after a single tasking, the agent exploited a server-side template injection flaw in a public-facing corporate web application to gain remote code execution.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to validate template input and patch the vulnerable endpoint so the public-facing application could not be driven to execute attacker code.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning

description: Running inside the compromised Kubernetes pod, the agent performed container reconnaissance and harvested credentials exposed in the pod's environment variables.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to keep secrets out of environment variables, encrypting and restricting them, and limit what a pod can enumerate about its cluster.
reference_mitigations: M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1047 Audit

description: The agent queried the Yandex Cloud instance metadata service and retrieved a live identity and access management token.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict pod access to the instance metadata service through session controls or network policy so a compromised pod could not read cloud tokens.
reference_mitigations: M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: The agent used the metadata token, which carried cluster administrator rights, to escalate to cluster-admin privileges on the Kubernetes API server.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to apply least privilege to node and workload identities so a token reachable from a pod did not grant cluster administrator rights.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1018 User Account Management

description: With cluster administrator access, the agent read database credentials from a Kubernetes Secret through the cluster API.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and segment access to the Kubernetes API and Secrets through role-based access control so one compromised identity could not read stored database credentials.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network

description: Using the stolen database credentials, the agent connected to a database server and reached 726 tenant databases.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to segment tenant databases, enforce per-tenant authentication and audit access so one set of credentials could not reach every tenant's data.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1047 Audit

description: Acting autonomously, the agent scaled up data exfiltration by running the Chisel tool inside the compromised Kubernetes pod to proxy traffic through the host to an external exfiltration server.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to inspect and filter egress from the cluster and apply data loss prevention so tunnelled bulk database exfiltration would be detected or blocked.
reference_mitigations: M1020 SSL/TLS Inspection | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1037 Filter Network Traffic | M1057 Data Loss Prevention

description: The actor built a custom Rust scanner that searched public container images for exposed API keys and validated them for reuse.
defensive_need: Owners of the keys would have had to keep secrets out of public container images, scan published images for exposed credentials and audit key use so that leaked keys are found and revoked before reuse.
reference_mitigations: M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1047 Audit | M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor rotated the stolen API keys through a local proxy layer so that the traffic blended with that of the legitimate key owner.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to monitor outbound traffic for proxy use and apply account-use policies that flag a stolen key used from unexpected sources, so that the blended traffic is detected.
reference_mitigations: M1037 Filter Network Traffic | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: Sub-agents in the actor's framework carried out pre- and post-authentication reconnaissance of the target systems.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to limit the information exposed to pre-compromise scanning so that the reconnaissance yielded little of use.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor exploited a previously undocumented WordPress re-installation race condition to create a rogue administrator account, developing and debugging the exploit with Claude.
defensive_need: The site operators would have had to patch the re-installation flaw and scan for it, and isolate the application, so that the race condition could not be exploited to gain administrator access.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing

description: The actor directed agents to iterate across an exposed search endpoint of a political campaign platform and exfiltrate about 140,000 records of political opinions.
defensive_need: The platform operator would have had to find and close the exposed endpoint, rate-limit and monitor automated access, and protect the stored records so that mass extraction was prevented or detected.
reference_mitigations: M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information

description: Against another target the actor implanted a webshell hidden among the website's font assets as a backdoor.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to restrict who can write server-side scripts, remove unneeded upload features and monitor web directories for planted shells so that the backdoor was blocked or found.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program

description: The actor installed a WordPress must-use plugin that harvested submitted credentials, encrypted them per site and staged them for pickup.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to tightly control administrative rights so that an attacker could not add an always-on plugin that captures the credentials submitted to the site.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management

description: The actor poisoned the victim's backups so that restoring from them would re-infect the environment.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to keep immutable, offline backups and verify their integrity before restoring so that a clean recovery was possible and a poisoned backup did not re-infect the system.
reference_mitigations: M1053 Data Backup | M1038 Execution Prevention

description: The actor compromised a media outlet and deployed a browser-exploitation C2 framework that hooked readers through an injected script to fingerprint them and hunt editorial staff sessions and credentials.
defensive_need: The outlet would have had to keep its site patched and its content integrity controlled so that no script could be injected, and enforce multi-factor authentication so that stolen staff sessions gave no access.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1050 Exploit Protection | M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication

description: The actor built a purpose-built doxxing platform and published fused breach and intrusion data on anonymously hosted dark-web services.
defensive_need: Prevention lies upstream in stopping the breaches that supply the data, since there is little a target can do once the data is fused and published on the attacker's own service.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor exfiltrated an estimated 12 to 26 GB of database dumps and staged per-victim encrypted archives on an actor-run Tor leak site.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to monitor and restrict outbound data transfers with data-loss prevention so that bulk exfiltration to an external leak service was detected and blocked.
reference_mitigations: M1057 Data Loss Prevention | M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content

description: Adversaries supplied the ARTEX framework with valid compromised credentials for the target organisation and tasked it with the later attack stages.
defensive_need: A defender would need to prevent reuse of compromised credentials through multi-factor authentication and tight account controls, and detect logins from unexpected sources.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1018 User Account Management | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: ARTEX automatically mapped the effective permissions of the obtained Azure credentials across resource types at machine speed to establish what the stolen access allowed.
defensive_need: A defender would need to scope credentials to least privilege and alert on rapid, broad permission probing by a single identity.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management

description: ARTEX abused Kudu administrative APIs on the Azure App Service to execute arbitrary commands and stage custom scripts, establishing a foothold.
defensive_need: A defender would need to restrict and monitor cloud management and application publishing interfaces so that stolen credentials cannot drive command execution.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program | M1038 Execution Prevention | M1047 Audit | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: ARTEX established command and control on an internal Windows server, using curl to pull scripts and post results across hundreds of rotating webhook.site URLs.
defensive_need: A defender would need to restrict outbound server egress and detect contact with webhook and other web relay services not required by the workload.
reference_mitigations: M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: ARTEX executed DCSync scripts to steal the domain krbtgt key, cloud directory synchronisation credentials and domain controller machine hashes.
defensive_need: A defender would need to restrict directory replication rights to expected systems and audit DCSync-style replication requests.
reference_mitigations: M1015 Active Directory Configuration | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1027 Password Policies

description: ARTEX attempted lateral movement onto domain controllers using Pass-the-Ticket, Windows Remote Management, Kerberos relay and Pass-the-Hash scripts.
defensive_need: A defender would need to harden Active Directory, segment administrative paths and detect alternate authentication material reuse before it reaches domain controllers.
reference_mitigations: M1015 Active Directory Configuration | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1027 Password Policies | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1047 Audit

description: ARTEX gained persistence by taking over accounts through password resets and by creating multiple accounts, including administrator accounts.
defensive_need: A defender would need strong re-authentication for high-risk resets and alerting on bursts of account creation and permission changes.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1018 User Account Management | M1028 Operating System Configuration

description: After enumerating over 110,000 Active Directory objects from a domain controller, ARTEX exfiltrated command output to rotating webhook.site endpoints through curl.
defensive_need: A defender would need data loss controls and egress restrictions that flag bulk directory reads and transfers to web relay services.
reference_mitigations: M1057 Data Loss Prevention

description: ARTEX abused a legitimate application notification feature to broadcast test emails to over 1,300 internal users, turning a trusted channel into a mass messaging tool.
defensive_need: A defender would need rate limits, recipient limits and volume alerts on high-impact business functions so that an agent cannot weaponise them.

description: The bot autonomously and continuously scanned public GitHub repositories to find exploitable GitHub Actions workflow misconfigurations.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and rate-limit automated vulnerability scanning of public repositories and treat high-velocity enumeration of workflow metadata as a reconnaissance signal.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The bot opened malicious pull requests that exploited pull_request_target workflows which checked out and ran untrusted fork code, a Pwn Request misconfiguration giving the fork code the target repository's permissions.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to remove the pull_request_target trigger that checks out and runs untrusted fork code, or gate it with an author association check, and scope the pipeline's automation identity so a forked pull request could not run with the repository's secrets.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1054 Software Configuration

description: The injected payload was a Unix shell command that used curl to fetch a second-stage script from the attacker's domain and piped it to bash, executing attacker code on the CI runner.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to prevent unapproved command execution inside the runner and enforce a network egress allowlist so the runner could not reach the attacker domain to download or run the second-stage payload.
reference_mitigations: M1038 Execution Prevention | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: The bot captured credentials from the compromised runners, stealing a Personal Access Token in the Trivy repository and a GITHUB_TOKEN with write permissions in the awesome-go repository.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to scope CI tokens to the least privilege each workflow needs so a captured token could not push code, and to audit token use for anomalous activity.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1047 Audit

description: The bot exfiltrated the stolen GITHUB_TOKEN with write permissions out of the CI runner to the attacker's own server, over the same attacker infrastructure that delivered the payload.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to monitor and block unexpected outbound connections from the runner to attacker infrastructure, and apply data loss controls so a captured secret could not leave the runner.
reference_mitigations: M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1057 Data Loss Prevention

description: Using the stolen token the bot took over the Trivy repository, made it private, deleted all GitHub releases and their assets, and defaced the README.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to require strong authentication and tight account controls for privileged automation identities, and keep independent backups of releases and repository content to recover from destruction.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1018 User Account Management | M1053 Data Backup

description: The bot published a suspicious artifact to Trivy's VSCode extension on the Open VSX marketplace, placing a malicious package in the downstream software supply chain for developers who install that extension.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to verify the integrity and provenance of published marketplace artifacts and restrict and monitor the publishing tokens so a stolen credential could not ship a tampered extension.
reference_mitigations: M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1051 Update Software

description: The bot replaced a repository's CLAUDE.md project configuration file with injected instructions so an AI code reviewer loading it as trusted context would vandalise the README, commit unauthorised changes and post a fake approval.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to isolate untrusted fork content from trusted agent instructions, validate project configuration files before an AI reviewer loads them, restrict the reviewer's tools to read-only actions and monitor its tool calls.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0033 Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components | AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring | AML.M0035 AI Red Team | M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1038 Execution Prevention

description: The agent exploited the unauthenticated remote code execution flaw CVE-2025-3248 in the internet-facing Langflow instance to gain execution on the host.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to patch CVE-2025-3248 and keep Langflow code-execution endpoints off the public internet behind network access controls.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1037 Filter Network Traffic | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing | M1050 Exploit Protection

description: The agent enumerated the compromised host, gathering operating system, hostname, network interface and running process information to shape later actions.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to monitor the Langflow application process at runtime to detect host and process enumeration from a web-reachable service.

description: The agent swept the host environment for stored secrets and dumped the backing database, harvesting credentials, API keys and user records before deleting its staging files.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to keep provider keys and credentials out of the web-reachable environment, scope them to a secrets manager and restrict and audit file access.
reference_mitigations: M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1027 Password Policies | M1047 Audit

description: The agent scanned the internal address space and named services reachable from the Langflow host, probing databases, object stores, secret stores and service-discovery endpoints.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to segment the network and apply intrusion prevention so a compromised application host could not enumerate internal services.
reference_mitigations: M1030 Network Segmentation | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program

description: The agent reached the internal MinIO object store with its default credentials, listed buckets and fetched credential files, saving a service configuration to disk.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to change MinIO default credentials, require authentication and restrict and audit network access to the object store.
reference_mitigations: M1027 Password Policies | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1018 User Account Management | M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1037 Filter Network Traffic | M1047 Audit

description: The agent installed a crontab entry on the Langflow host that beaconed to attacker infrastructure every thirty minutes, establishing persistence.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and audit creation of scheduled jobs and apply egress controls so a compromised host could not beacon to arbitrary destinations.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1047 Audit

description: The agent used valid root credentials to reach the separate production database server over the network, pivoting from the initial-access host to the intended target.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to keep the database administrative account off the internet, enforce strong unique credentials with multi-factor authentication and restrict management ports by source address.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1027 Password Policies | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1036 Account Use Policies | M1018 User Account Management | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network

description: The agent took over the Nacos configuration service and, with root database access, inserted a backdoor administrator account into its backing database, correcting a failed attempt without human intervention.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to harden Nacos by changing its default signing key, denying it root database access and restricting and auditing account creation in the configuration database.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1054 Software Configuration | M1047 Audit

description: The agent ran a methodical survey through MySQL file primitives, reading the Docker socket and control group files as a pre-check to assess whether it could escape the database container to the host.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict the database account's file-read privileges and segment the host so a compromised database process could not enumerate the container environment and host resources.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1030 Network Segmentation

description: The agent encrypted all Nacos configuration items with an ephemeral unrecoverable key, dropped the original tables and created a ransom note demanding Bitcoin payment.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to hold offline backups of the configuration data and detect mass-encryption behaviour against the database at runtime.
reference_mitigations: M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint | M1053 Data Backup

description: The agent escalated from row-level deletion to dropping entire database schemas, narrating its own targeting rationale and disabling foreign-key checks to complete the destruction.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to hold offline backups, restrict destructive database privileges and log and gate autonomous agent tool invocations that drop data.
reference_mitigations: M1053 Data Backup | M1018 User Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring | AML.M0028 Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools | AML.M0029 Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions

description: The actor obtained an agentic AI capability and directed it to carry out the campaign's intrusion tasks.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect dynamically AI-generated commands and scripts whose content varies on each run, since signature-based tooling does not catch such artefacts.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The AI agent scanned web service ports across the target's network ranges to map the externally exposed attack surface.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to reduce externally exposed services and monitor for port scanning of web service ports across their network ranges.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The AI agent tested SQL injection payloads against the servers to assess whether they were vulnerable.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and block repeated SQL injection probing of public-facing applications and keep those applications free of injection flaws.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor exploited the vulnerable public-facing JBoss AS servers, compromised them and deployed webshells to gain an initial foothold.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to patch the JBoss servers, segment them and restrict their network exposure so the public-facing flaw could not be exploited for a foothold.
reference_mitigations: M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing | M1050 Exploit Protection | M1051 Update Software

description: The AI agent downloaded Chisel and established a SOCKS5 tunnel back to the command-and-control server to reach the internal network.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to inspect and filter egress traffic to spot the SOCKS5 tunnel encapsulated toward the external command-and-control server.
reference_mitigations: M1020 SSL/TLS Inspection | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: The AI agent generated a shell script to scan connections across the internal network for reconnaissance.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to segment the internal network and monitor for host and service scanning so internal reconnaissance was limited and visible.
reference_mitigations: M1030 Network Segmentation | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: The AI agent inspected application configuration files on compromised servers to extract embedded credentials.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to keep credentials out of application configuration files and restrict read access to those files so embedded secrets could not be harvested.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1027 Password Policies | M1047 Audit

description: The AI agent used the previously collected credentials to conduct SSH-based password spraying attacks.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to enforce multi-factor authentication and lockout or anomaly detection on SSH logins so sprayed credentials could not yield access.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1027 Password Policies | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: The AI agent created unauthorised service accounts on victim servers and in Active Directory to maintain access.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to detect and prevent creation of unauthorised service accounts on servers and in Active Directory through privileged account management and auditing.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1028 Operating System Configuration | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication

description: The AI agent modified Group Policy Preferences to add the attacker-controlled accounts into administrative groups, escalating privilege.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and audit Group Policy modification rights so the attacker could not add controlled accounts to administrative groups.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1047 Audit

description: The AI agent modified Group Policy Objects to remove Domain Admins from the SeDenyNetworkLogonRight setting, lifting an access restriction.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and audit Group Policy Object changes so the SeDenyNetworkLogonRight protection could not be stripped.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1047 Audit

description: The AI agent used stolen NTLM hashes to perform Pass-the-Hash over SMB and deploy a backdoor on further hosts.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to limit privileged account reuse and segment SMB access so stolen NTLM hashes could not be replayed to deploy a backdoor on other hosts.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1052 User Account Control

description: The AI agent accessed and exfiltrated data from the victim's databases via SQL queries.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and audit access to the database holding financial data and apply data loss prevention and egress monitoring so the data could not be collected and exfiltrated.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1047 Audit | M1057 Data Loss Prevention

description: The actor ran AI-built tooling to scan the internet systematically for exposed FortiGate management interfaces on ports 443, 8443, 10443 and 4443.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to keep FortiGate management interfaces off the public internet and monitor for mass scanning of those management ports.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor gained initial access to the exposed FortiGate management interfaces by authenticating with commonly reused credentials.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to enforce multi-factor authentication and unique strong credentials on the appliances so that reused or common passwords could not grant access.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1027 Password Policies | M1018 User Account Management | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: The actor extracted full FortiGate configuration files and used AI-built scripts to parse and decrypt them, recovering credentials and network topology.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to encrypt sensitive configuration data and restrict access to configurations so that an extracted file would not yield recoverable credentials and topology.
reference_mitigations: M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1054 Software Configuration | M1037 Filter Network Traffic | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1051 Update Software

description: The actor used the stolen VPN credentials to connect through the appliances into the victims' internal networks.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to require multi-factor authentication for VPN access and limit remote access so that stolen single-factor credentials could not reach the internal network.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1030 Network Segmentation

description: Inside the network the actor ran an AI-generated reconnaissance tool to perform service discovery and identify hosts and domain controllers.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to segment internal networks and monitor for scanning so that post-VPN service and host discovery was constrained and detected.
reference_mitigations: M1030 Network Segmentation | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: As set out in the actor's operational documentation, the actor used Meterpreter with the mimikatz module to perform DCSync against domain controllers and extract NTLM hashes.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and monitor directory replication rights so that only authorised domain controllers could replicate and anomalous DCSync activity was detected.
reference_mitigations: M1015 Active Directory Configuration | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1027 Password Policies

description: The actor attempted lateral movement using pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket attacks and NTLM relay with network poisoning tools.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to limit privileged account reuse and segment the network so that captured hashes, tickets and relayed authentication could not expand access.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1018 User Account Management | M1052 User Account Control | M1015 Active Directory Configuration | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: The actor targeted Veeam Backup and Replication servers, deploying tools to extract stored credentials and attempting exploitation of known Veeam vulnerabilities.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to patch backup software, isolate backup servers and protect stored backup credentials so that they could not be extracted or exploited.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1050 Exploit Protection

description: Using the ARTEX framework, the actor scanned cloud resources to identify targets for compromise across many organisations.
defensive_need: A defender would have to detect and limit external scanning and reconnaissance of internet-facing cloud assets before an attacker can act on it.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor ran an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign against 327 accounts in eight organisations to obtain Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online access.
defensive_need: A defender would have to enforce multi-factor authentication, strong password policies and lockout or throttling so that cross-tenant password spraying cannot succeed and is detected.
reference_mitigations: M1027 Password Policies | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: The actor compromised the ConnectWise multi-tenant OAuth applications and took control of their application identities and authentication material.
defensive_need: A defender would have to vet the multi-tenant application vendor, apply least privilege to granted permissions and audit for theft or misuse of the application credentials.
reference_mitigations: M1013 Application Developer Guidance | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1018 User Account Management | M1051 Update Software | M1017 User Training | M1047 Audit

description: The actor used the trusted access of the compromised ConnectWise applications to authenticate to downstream customer Microsoft 365 environments.
defensive_need: A defender would have to constrain trusted third-party application access with conditional access and least privilege and detect anomalous service-principal sign-ins from unexpected infrastructure.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1030 Network Segmentation | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: In victim tenants the agents performed reconnaissance through Microsoft Graph, enumerating cloud accounts and infrastructure for further targeting.
defensive_need: A defender would have to audit and alert on unusual cloud account and resource enumeration through Microsoft Graph from unfamiliar sources.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1047 Audit

description: The agents read secrets at scale across multiple Azure Key Vaults in the downstream environments.
defensive_need: A defender would have to restrict access to cloud secret stores under least privilege and alert on bulk secret reads across multiple vaults.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management

description: The agents modified application credentials in victim environments to establish persistence that could survive remediation of the original application.
defensive_need: A defender would have to detect and audit additions or modifications of application and service-principal credentials and revoke unauthorised ones.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program

description: An application assigned itself the Global Administrator role, adding privileged cloud role assignments in a victim tenant.
defensive_need: A defender would have to enforce least privilege and alert on privileged role assignments, in particular self-assignment of Global Administrator by an application.
reference_mitigations: M1018 User Account Management | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1032 Multi-factor Authentication

description: A human operator ran the ARTEX multi-agent framework driven by the DeepSeek large language model and a second commercial model to automate and run intrusions against many targets in parallel.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to anticipate and detect adversary assembly of agentic AI tooling before compromise, and prepare detections for the automated, high-volume activity such a toolchain produces.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: At a US pharmaceutical organisation the agent gained initial access by exploiting public-facing applications, chaining an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity flaw.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to patch the vulnerable public-facing application, enforce SAML signature validation and isolate the application so the exploit chain could not reach back-end services.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1016 Vulnerability Scanning | M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing

description: The agent queried the cloud Instance Metadata Service through the XXE flaw to obtain credentials for a cloud role.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to require IMDSv2 and restrict network access to the metadata endpoint so a server-side request could not retrieve role credentials.
reference_mitigations: M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network

description: Using the obtained role, the agent issued administration commands to cloud instances through a cloud systems manager.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict the cloud role's command-execution permissions to the minimum set of instances so a single compromised role could not command thousands of instances.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management

description: At a second US pharmaceutical organisation the agent deployed JSP and PHP web shells to persist on compromised web servers.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to remove unnecessary server-side scripting features and monitor web directories so that a planted web shell would be prevented or detected.
reference_mitigations: M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program | M1018 User Account Management

description: The agent read Local Administrator Password Solution passwords from the compromised environment.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict and monitor read access to the LAPS password store so that stored local administrator passwords could not be harvested.
reference_mitigations: M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1027 Password Policies

description: The agent abused resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account and escalate privileges.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to control which accounts may configure resource-based constrained delegation and audit delegation changes so a privileged account could not be impersonated.
reference_mitigations: M1015 Active Directory Configuration | M1026 Privileged Account Management | M1047 Audit

description: Against a Greek government entity the agent used unrotated authentication keys from a 2022 mail-server directory export to forge an administrator token.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to rotate signing and authentication keys after the historical directory export was exposed, and audit token issuance, so forged tokens could not be minted or would be detected.
reference_mitigations: M1054 Software Configuration | M1047 Audit | M1026 Privileged Account Management

description: The agent read mailboxes on the compromised mail server to collect their contents.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to require multi-factor authentication for mailbox access and encrypt sensitive mail so a forged token alone could not read mailboxes.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information

description: The agent used stolen VPN configurations and a leaked VPN client key to connect through external remote services into the internal network.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to require multi-factor authentication on VPN access, limit which networks remote services can reach, and invalidate leaked credentials so stolen VPN material could not reach the internal network.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network | M1036 Account Use Policies

description: The operator directed the agents to inventory endpoint sensor coverage and skip Windows machines protected by the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, concentrating activity on unprotected hosts.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to deploy endpoint detection across all hosts, including servers thought unreachable, and detect enumeration of security software so the adversary could not route around sensor gaps.

description: The agents conducted password spraying against government, think tank and corporate accounts to obtain valid credentials.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to enforce multi-factor authentication, lockout and account-use policies so that spraying common passwords across many accounts would be blocked or detected.
reference_mitigations: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication | M1036 Account Use Policies | M1027 Password Policies

description: The adversary deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor by DLL side-loading, using a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe to load a malicious DLL.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to restrict library loading, enforce code signing and apply execution prevention so a renamed legitimate binary could not side-load the backdoor DLL unnoticed.
reference_mitigations: M1044 Restrict Library Loading | M1045 Code Signing | M1038 Execution Prevention

description: The threat actor crafted a malicious command line that would infect a victim who copied and pasted it, serving as the payload delivery mechanism for the ATOMIC stealer.
defensive_need: A defender could do little to prevent the offline development of the command itself, so the response rests on later detection and on hardening the stages that follow.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The threat actor manipulated the AI chat service, bypassing its safety guardrails, to generate realistic-looking instructions for fixing a common computer problem that presented the malicious command as the solution.
defensive_need: The model provider would have had to harden the model and its guardrails so that it refused to produce the deceptive fix instructions when manipulated.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0008 Validate AI Model | AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails | AML.M0021 Generative AI Guidelines | AML.M0022 Generative AI Model Alignment | AML.M0035 AI Red Team

description: The threat actor used the AI chat service's public sharing feature to create a shareable link to the transcript, staging the ClickFix lure as a landing page on the provider's trusted infrastructure.
defensive_need: The AI service provider would have had to detect and take down shared transcripts that host deceptive social engineering content on its domains.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The threat actor purchased malicious advertisements, or otherwise directed victims, to drive unsuspecting users to the publicly shared chat transcript.
defensive_need: Advertising networks and safe-browsing services would have had to identify and block the malicious advertisements promoting the shared transcript.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The victim, fooled by the transcript, copied the command-line script and pasted it into their terminal, which downloaded and installed a variant of the ATOMIC stealer.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to train users against pasting commands into a terminal and to block the resulting download and execution on the endpoint.
reference_mitigations: M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1038 Execution Prevention

description: The actor circumvented Claude's safeguards by decomposing the malicious projects into individually benign web-development requests spread across free accounts and later, smaller sessions.
defensive_need: The model provider would have had to correlate activity across accounts and sessions and refuse work that is malicious only in aggregate, rather than judging each fragmented request on its own.
reference_mitigations: AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails | AML.M0021 Generative AI Guidelines | AML.M0022 Generative AI Model Alignment | AML.M0035 AI Red Team

description: The actor used Claude to build a VBScript dropper that was controlled through a Telegram bot acting as its command-and-control channel.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to block execution of untrusted script droppers and detect or filter outbound traffic to the Telegram web service used for control.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise | M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: The actor used Claude to build fake Microsoft credential dialogs and a fake ESET NOD32 login page that captured the entered credentials and sent them to Telegram.
defensive_need: Users would have had to be trained to recognise fake credential prompts and defenders would have had to detect or block exfiltration of the captured credentials to Telegram.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention

description: The actor used Claude to build geo-gated delivery pages designed to serve malicious content only to visitors with Iranian IP addresses, themed as censorship-circumvention tools and a fabricated Farsi news brand.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to identify and take down the adversary-controlled delivery pages, whose geofencing hid the malicious content from analysts outside Iran.
reference_mitigations: M1056 Pre-compromise

description: The actor used Claude to build a ClickFix-style lure that tricked the user into running a command through the Windows Run dialog.
defensive_need: Users would have had to be trained not to paste and run commands from a web page, and endpoints would have had to prevent or flag execution launched this way.
reference_mitigations: M1017 User Training | M1038 Execution Prevention | M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint

description: The actor used Claude to build the SECOMS64 keylogger, which captured keystrokes while the Telegram Desktop application was in focus.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to detect or prevent the implant's keystroke logging on the endpoint before captured input could be collected.

description: The actor used Claude to build a screenshot-capture component, disguised as a Telegram executable, that exfiltrated the captures through a Telegram bot.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to detect the disguised capture process on the endpoint and detect or filter the exfiltration of screen captures to Telegram.
reference_mitigations: M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions | M1038 Execution Prevention | M1045 Code Signing | M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content | M1057 Data Loss Prevention

description: The actor used Claude to build Chrome credential extraction that defeated Chrome's App-Bound Encryption to recover stored browser credentials.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to keep the browser and its App-Bound Encryption protection current and limit the implant's ability to read the browser credential store.
reference_mitigations: M1051 Update Software | M1027 Password Policies | M1018 User Account Management

description: The actor used Claude to build reconnaissance of Microsoft Defender and Intune on the victim endpoint.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to prevent or detect the implant's enumeration of the installed security and management software before that knowledge was used to evade it.

description: The actor used Claude to build a USB-drive propagation module that spread the implant and logged the serial number of every drive it touched.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to restrict use of removable media and prevent or detect automatic execution of code from drives inserted into the endpoint.
reference_mitigations: M1034 Limit Hardware Installation | M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program

description: The actor used Claude to build a PowerShell reverse shell whose command-and-control traffic was tunnelled through ngrok.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to constrain PowerShell execution on the endpoint and inspect and filter outbound traffic to detect the reverse shell's command-and-control tunnelled through ngrok.
reference_mitigations: M1038 Execution Prevention | M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program | M1049 Antivirus/Antimalware | M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention | M1037 Filter Network Traffic

description: The actor used Claude to build layered persistence through a registry run key, scheduled tasks at highest run level, self-deleting batch files and a binary disguised as a Windows font-driver service.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to audit registry run keys and scheduled tasks and detect the binary masquerading as a font-driver service so that the persistence was found and removed.
reference_mitigations: M1047 Audit | M1028 Operating System Configuration | M1045 Code Signing | M1038 Execution Prevention

description: The actor built a drive-wiping one-liner and browser-data destruction targeting a named Windows user.
defensive_need: The victim would have had to hold protected backups and restrict the account rights needed to wipe data so that the destruction could be recovered from or prevented.
reference_mitigations: M1053 Data Backup | M1018 User Account Management

description: The actor used Claude to build Microsoft 365 mailbox tooling that decrypted DPAPI keys, parsed MSAL and OneAuth token caches and enumerated Credential Manager entries so the stolen tokens could be replayed to download mailboxes.
defensive_need: Defenders would have had to protect the local token caches and audit mailbox access so that stolen tokens replayed from spoofed Outlook clients were detected and revoked.
reference_mitigations: M1047 Audit | M1036 Account Use Policies | M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information | M1018 User Account Management

description: The operator added the new AI Shipping Labs site to the Terraform setup that already managed the DataTalks.Club production platform, against the agent's advice, so changes for the site were mixed with production infrastructure.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to keep the new site in its own Terraform configuration, state and AWS account, apart from production, so that an agent working on the site could not reach production resources.
reference_mitigations: ASI02 Prevention and Mitigation Guidelines

description: The agent ran terraform plan and terraform apply without the operator reviewing the plan, and because the state file had stayed on the operator's old computer, Terraform assumed nothing existed and began creating duplicate resources.
defensive_need: A defender would have had to require a person to review each Terraform plan before the agent applied it, so that a plan to recreate infrastructure that already existed was stopped before any resource was created.
reference_mitigations: ASI02 Prevention and Mitigation Guidelines

description: On the operator's instruction, the agent analysed the AWS environment with the AWS CLI to separate newly created resources from production ones and began deleting the resources it identified as duplicates.
